records.place: Monte Bello Ridge above Cupertino, Santa Cruz Mountains, California

wine.name: Monte Bello
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the larger part, with Merlot and smaller shares of Petit Verdot and Cabernet Franc; the blend changes with the vintage.
wine.sites: The Monte Bello vineyard on the ridge above the San Andreas fault, from about 400 to over 800 metres up, on fractured limestone under a layer of weathered greenstone and clay.
wine.making: Each parcel is fermented apart with the vineyard's own yeasts and goes through its malolactic fermentation naturally. The lots are then tasted and only a part of them chosen for Monte Bello; the blend is raised in barrels of air dried American oak, with a little French, and bottled after well over a year in wood.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackberry and plum over cedar, tobacco and violet, with an iron edge and, when young, a touch of vanilla from the American oak; leather and anise come with age, over firm, fine tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first ten years or so, it unfolds slowly over decades, as the 1971 showed when it was poured again thirty years after Paris.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The vineyard on Monte Bello Ridge, first planted in the 1880s, and the name of the wine drawn from it.
The appellation: the range between San Francisco Bay and the Pacific, south of the city and well away from Napa.
Ridge lists on its back labels every ingredient used in making the wine, a habit of the house since the 2011 vintage.

records.table: Monte Bello is Ridge Vineyards' Cabernet led blend from a limestone ridge high in the Santa Cruz Mountains, raised in American oak. Its 1971 placed fifth in Paris in 1976 and first when the same wines were poured again in 2006, so give it years and a decanter.
records.story: In 1885 a San Francisco doctor bought land high on Monte Bello Ridge, planted vines and built a winery, ready for the vintage of 1892, as Ridge tells it. By the 1940s his winery had closed and its vines were abandoned. In 1949 a theologian who had bought an old winery and vineyard just below replanted Cabernet Sauvignon there, and those vines would make the first Ridge wines. In 1959 a small group of engineers from the Stanford Research Institute bought his land, and in 1962 they bonded its winery again as Ridge Vineyards and made the first commercial Monte Bello; in 1968 they bought the doctor's old winery as well. A winemaker who joined them in 1969 led the cellar until 2016, holding to native yeasts, American oak and what the house calls pre-industrial winemaking. At the Paris tasting of May 1976, before French judges, the 1971 Monte Bello placed fifth among ten reds of Bordeaux and California. At the end of 1986 Ridge became part of the Japanese Otsuka group, which promised, as Ridge tells it, to leave the business as it was. Thirty years after Paris, in 2006, the same wines were poured blind again, and the 1971 placed first. It is the wine to pour when a guest asks whether California Cabernet can age.

traps: Monte Bello grows in the Santa Cruz Mountains south of San Francisco, not in Napa, though it stood beside Napa's wines in Paris.
Its American oak points blind tasters towards a warm region or towards Rioja, yet the vineyard is high and cool.
The 1971 Monte Bello placed fifth in Paris in 1976 and first at the tasting of 2006; the red that won in 1976 was Stag's Leap Wine Cellars' 1973.

cards.front: Ridge Monte Bello: what soil lies under the vineyard, and what fault runs below the ridge?
cards.back: Fractured limestone under weathered greenstone and clay, high above the San Andreas fault.

cards.front: Which Japanese group did Ridge Vineyards join at the end of 1986?
cards.back: The Otsuka group, a pharmaceutical company.

questions.q: A guest tastes Monte Bello blind and guesses a warm region from its vanilla. What explains the vanilla?

New French barriques from Burgundy
Oak chips added during fermentation
Large old casks of Slavonian oak
questions.exp: Ridge raises Monte Bello mostly in air dried American oak, which gives the vanilla; the vineyard itself is high and cool, and French barrels play only a small part.

opts: Ridge Monte Bello 1971
Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973

records.place: Mount Harlan, in the Gavilan Mountains of San Benito County, California

wine.name: Calera Jensen Vineyard Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from vines planted in 1975.
wine.sites: The Jensen vineyard, the largest of the three parcels planted in 1975, on limestone rich hillside soil at about 670 metres on Mount Harlan, some twenty five miles east of Monterey Bay.
wine.making: Fermented as whole clusters with native yeasts in open fermenters, punched down and pressed after a fortnight or more in the house's gravity flow winery. The wine then spends sixteen to eighteen months in French oak barrels, about a third of them new.
wine.glass: Dark red cherry, wild strawberry and black raspberry, with the rosehip and orange peel of the house and touches of red tea and sassafras; wiry acidity and fine, firm tannin, with autumn leaves as it ages.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first five years or so, it lasts fifteen to twenty years in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems closed, an old one gently off its sediment; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The appellation approved in 1990, drawn around Calera's limestone vineyards high in the Gavilan Mountains.
The largest of the three parcels planted in 1975, named, by the house's account, for the founder's father.
Spanish for lime kiln, after the old lime kiln on the property.

records.table: Calera's Jensen Vineyard Pinot Noir comes from one of three limestone parcels planted in 1975, high on Mount Harlan, inland from the coast. Whole clusters and native yeasts give a wiry, long lived Pinot Noir of cherry, rosehip and orange peel.
records.story: Calera grew out of a search for limestone. Its founder, Josh Jensen (1944 to 2022), worked harvests in Burgundy and came home convinced that Pinot Noir needs limestone soil, which is rare in California. His search ended high in the Gavilan Mountains of San Benito County, at a property where limestone had once been quarried and burnt, and he bought it in 1974. The old lime kiln there gave the house its name, calera being Spanish for lime kiln. In 1975 he planted three parcels of Pinot Noir, Selleck, Reed and Jensen, the largest, named by the house's account for his father; the first crop came in 1978. In 1990 Mount Harlan was approved as an appellation of its own, drawn around Calera's vineyards. The house restored the old kiln in 1997, as it tells the story, and in 2017 the founder sold Calera to the Duckhorn group; he died in 2022, aged 78. Jensen, the parcel that bears the family name, is the bottle to open when a guest asks whether California soil can speak as clearly as Burgundy's.

others.name: Selleck Pinot Noir
others.note: From another of the three parcels planted in 1975, smaller than Jensen and bottled on its own.

others.name: Mt. Harlan Viognier
others.note: From vines first planted in 1983, among the early plantings of Viognier in California.

traps: Mount Harlan lies some twenty five miles inland in San Benito County, not on the coast; height keeps it cool, with marine air drawn in from Monterey Bay.
Calera is Spanish for lime kiln: the name points to the limestone, not to a family or a place on the coast.
Jensen, Selleck and Reed are parcels of the house's own estate on Mount Harlan, not vineyards bought from growers.

cards.front: Calera: what does the Spanish name mean, and why was it chosen?
cards.back: Lime kiln, after the old kiln on the Mount Harlan property, where limestone was once quarried and burnt.

cards.front: In which year was the Mount Harlan appellation approved, and whose vineyards does it hold?

questions.q: A guest asks why Calera's Jensen Vineyard Pinot Noir stays so fresh though it grows inland. What do you tell them?

A vineyard on the shore of Monterey Bay
Ageing in stainless steel rather than oak
White grapes blended in for lift
questions.exp: Jensen lies at about 670 metres in the Gavilan Mountains, and the height, with marine air from the bay, keeps it cool; the vineyard is some twenty five miles inland, not on the shore.

questions.q: What drew Calera's founder to a remote hilltop in San Benito County in 1974?

An old winery standing empty since Prohibition

The barrel time is sixteen months on the 2013 sheet and eighteen on recent ones, both a third new; the kiln restored in 1997 rests on the house's own page alone and is hedged.

records.place: Santa Maria Valley, Santa Barbara County, California

wine.name: Au Bon Climat Isabelle Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from several vineyards.
wine.sites: A selection of barrels that changes with the year: Bien Nacido in Santa Maria Valley, Sanford and Benedict in Sta. Rita Hills, Los Alamos and others, in some years reaching north to Anderson Valley and the Sonoma Coast.
wine.making: Each small lot is fermented apart in open fermenters, punched down by hand once or twice a day and moved only by gravity, never pumped. The lots age in new French oak barrels from François Frères for twenty to twenty four months, and the barrels for Isabelle are chosen by tasting over several months.
wine.glass: Red cherry, wild strawberry and candied cranberry with white pepper, cinnamon and a lift of jasmine; fresh acidity and fine tannin keep it lean and savoury rather than lush.
wine.ageing: Tight on release, it opens after four or five years and lasts fifteen years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if it seems closed; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The selection of chosen barrels from several vineyards, named for the founder's daughter.
French for a well exposed vineyard, borrowing Burgundy's word climat for a named site.
The appellation of most vintages, the barrels coming from more than one county; a few vintages read Santa Barbara County.

records.table: Isabelle is Au Bon Climat's Pinot Noir of chosen barrels, drawn from several vineyards, among them Bien Nacido and Sanford and Benedict, and raised entirely in new French oak. It is lean and savoury, red cherry and white pepper, made to sit beside food.
records.story: Jim Clendenen (1953 to 2021) began as an assistant winemaker at Zaca Mesa with the harvest of 1978, then worked vintages in Australia and France, as the house tells it, and came back sure that Santa Barbara County could make wine in the manner of Burgundy. With a partner he made the first Au Bon Climat from the harvest of 1982, in a converted dairy barn at the Los Alamos vineyard; the name, the house says, means a well exposed vineyard. At the start of the 1990s the partner left to found a winery of his own, and Clendenen carried on alone. He bought grapes from the cool valleys of the county that run from east to west, made Bien Nacido a vineyard name, and later moved his cellar into a winery on that vineyard, shared with Qupé. While others chased ripeness he held to lean, savoury wines made for the table. In the mid 1990s he began Isabelle, a selection of his chosen barrels of Pinot Noir from all his sources, named for his daughter. After his death in 2021 his son and daughter carried the house on. Isabelle is the wine to pour when a guest believes California Pinot Noir must be ripe and heavy.

records.place: Adelaida District, Paso Robles, Central Coast, California

wine.name: Esprit de Tablas
wine.grapes: Mourvèdre in the lead, often two fifths to a half, with Grenache, Syrah and a little Counoise.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyard on the limestone hillsides of the Adelaida District west of Paso Robles, planted from cuttings brought from Château de Beaucastel and grown on in the estate's nursery.
wine.making: Each variety is fermented apart with native yeasts, in large wooden upright vats, open tanks and closed steel tanks. The lots chosen for Esprit are blended in the spring after the harvest, then aged about a further year in French oak foudres of some 4,500 litres before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, plum and red currant over new leather, black tea, fennel and star anise, with a chalky grip; savoury rather than sweet, with firm, fine tannin and fresh acidity from the cool nights.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of release, it gains over five to ten, and strong vintages last twenty years and more, by the house's own tastings back to 2000.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The estate's leading red blend, called Esprit de Beaucastel until the name changed with the 2011 vintage.
One of eleven appellations created within Paso Robles in 2014, in the hills of its western side.
The wider appellation of San Luis Obispo County, of which the Adelaida District is part.

records.table: Esprit de Tablas is Tablas Creek Vineyard's Mourvèdre led red, grown on Paso Robles limestone from vines brought over from Château de Beaucastel. Think of it as Châteauneuf grammar in California: leather, plum and fennel, savoury and firm, at its ease with roast lamb.
records.story: In 1989 the Perrin family of Château de Beaucastel in Châteauneuf-du-Pape and their American importer, Robert Haas (1927 to 2018), bought land in the hills west of Paso Robles after searching California for soil and climate like Beaucastel's: limestone, warm, sunny days and cool nights. They named it for the creek that runs through it. They brought vine cuttings from Beaucastel itself, and from 1990 these spent some three years in the quarantine and testing of the United States Department of Agriculture, and the partners then set up a nursery on the estate to graft and grow them. The first vines went into the ground in 1994, and the first red came from the harvest of 1997. The nursery went on to supply Rhône cuttings to many other American growers. The flagship was named Esprit de Beaucastel from the 2000 vintage and took its own name, Esprit de Tablas, with the 2011, so that the estate would stand apart from Beaucastel. In 2014 its hills became the Adelaida District, one of eleven new appellations within Paso Robles, and Haas died in 2018, aged 90. Esprit is the California wine to pour beside a Châteauneuf when a guest asks what Mourvèdre brings.

others.note: The white counterpart, a Roussanne led blend from the same estate vineyard.

others.name: Côtes de Tablas

traps: The cuttings came from Château de Beaucastel itself, not from French nurseries in general, and passed through American quarantine before planting.
Esprit de Tablas leads with Mourvèdre, unlike most California Rhône blends, which lead with Grenache or Syrah.
Esprit de Beaucastel was this wine's earlier name in Paso Robles, never a wine of Château de Beaucastel in Châteauneuf.

wine.name: Le Cigare Volant
wine.grapes: Grenache in the lead in most years, with Syrah, Cinsault and Mourvèdre; the shares, and in some years the leading grape, change with the vintage.
wine.sites: Bought grapes from vineyards across the Central Coast, Monterey County among them, since the house's first vineyard at Bonny Doon in the Santa Cruz Mountains was given up.
wine.making: The method has changed over the years. The 2012 and the 2015 were raised partly in puncheons and large wooden uprights, the 2015 in part also in five gallon glass demijohns, while a later release was aged in stainless steel tanks and bottled ten months after the harvest.
wine.glass: Kirsch, raspberry and red plum with white pepper and wild thyme; medium bodied and moderate in alcohol rather than heavy, with fresh acidity and supple tannin.
wine.ageing: Generous within two or three years of the vintage, it keeps for a decade and more, as the house's own tastings of older vintages show.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant a young bottle, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Le Cigare Volant is Bonny Doon Vineyard's homage to Châteauneuf-du-Pape, a Grenache led blend first made in 1984 and named for the flying cigars a Châteauneuf decree of 1954 forbade to land. Expect kirsch, white pepper and wild thyme, at its ease with roast chicken.
records.story: In 1954 the village council of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, uneasy at reports of flying saucers, passed an order that barred them from landing in its vineyards; in French such a craft was a flying cigar. Bonny Doon Vineyard was founded in 1983 at Bonny Doon in the Santa Cruz Mountains and its founder soon turned to the grapes of the Rhône. In 1984 he made the first Le Cigare Volant, a blend of Châteauneuf's principal varieties grown under California conditions, as the house puts it, and released it in 1986 with a flying saucer on its label. He became a leading voice of the Rhône Rangers, the California growers of Rhône grapes, and from the start of the 2000s an early convert to the screwcap, for wines meant to age as well as for wines to drink young. The first vineyard at Bonny Doon was given up, and the wine has long been made from bought grapes across the Central Coast. In 2020 the founder sold the Bonny Doon brand, Le Cigare Volant with it, and at first stayed on as its winemaker. Pour it when a guest asks how Châteauneuf's grapes taste when grown in California.

The house took up screwcaps for wines meant to age, not only for wines to drink young.

report: Searches for this record: five of the group's 28 (the nineteenth to the twenty second and the twenty eighth), two restricted to bonnydoonvineyard.com; no fetch tried.
The house gives 1984 for the first vintage and 1986 for its release, Decanter and Wikipedia agreeing; the order of 1954 rests on the house's own pages, Decanter and The Drinks Business.

The screwcap is dated to the 2000 vintage of the Cigare in one account and to 2001 for the house in Wikipedia, so the story says the start of the 2000s; the mock funeral of the cork was found in no source and is left out.
The loss of the first vineyard to Pierce's disease, often dated 1994, was found in no source read, so the story follows the library's given up.

The sale of 2020 rests on Wikipedia and the house's sheet of 2023, which still names the founder as director of winemaking; the buyer is not named, and a Wine Spectator notice whose title names the living founder is not cited.

The blend and the vessels change: the 2012 was Mourvèdre led and raised partly in puncheons, the 2015 partly in glass demijohns, the 2023 Grenache led in steel, by the house's sheets; the record says so rather than give one recipe.
The glass rests on the library's kirsch and herbs and the Grenache led blend, as no tasting note was searched; the sale of Big House and Cardinal Zin and the cover story of 1989 are left out.
The founder's first aim of Pinot Noir to rival Burgundy stood in Wikipedia alone and is cut; the turn to the Rhône rests on the house's own timeline.

changed: wine.making: puncheons of 500 litres lose their size, not found; the vessels are tied to their vintages by the house's pages, the 2012 and the 2015 partly in puncheons and large wooden uprights, the 2015 also partly in glass demijohns, and the 2023 is no longer named but called a later release, aged in steel and bottled ten months after the harvest, so that no recent vintage is reported.

story: after some thirty six years is cut, the founding of 1983 to the sale of January 2020 making nearer thirty seven; stayed on to make the wine becomes at first stayed on as its winemaker, Decanter and the reports of the sale giving him winemaker and partner, a later column only an adviser without a title.

open: The founding year 1983 is the library's and most accounts'; one account gives 1981 and another 1982.
The loss of the first vineyard: Pierce's disease in 1994 in one account, phylloxera in another; the story keeps given up.
The screwcap: the 2000 Cigare in one account, 2001 for the house in another, and the cork's funeral of 2002 in one; the story keeps the start of the 2000s.
The founder first set out to make Pinot Noir, by Wine Spectator and Wikipedia; the author's cut is kept, the story beginning with the Rhone.
